title: Blood by Tube
passage:
Carriers drop out of the wall into a padded bin, one a minute. Jocelyn Ashvenor, a senior biomedical scientist, holds a spun tube to the window. Above the packed cells the plasma is pink.

“That pink is haemoglobin, from the cells,” she says. “They’ve burst on the way over, and their potassium is out in the plasma, so the number I’d report is higher than the patient’s.” Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning.

Last winter Ashvenor taped an accelerometer into a carrier and sent it round the loop for a week. Between stations the trace barely moved. “It’s the stop at the far end that does it,” she says. The loop runs at the speed it always has. What changed is the bins: two are lined with foam, and rejects are down by about half. Blood gases have never gone by tube; a porter walks those down.

– Cheryl Ludlow

questions.prompt: What does Ashvenor say about the samples sent by tube?

options.text: The number of rejected samples fell once the loop was slowed down.
A spoilt sample can be spotted by its colour before it leaves the ward.
Samples for blood gases go by tube because they cannot be left waiting.
The harm is done at the moment a carrier reaches the far end.

questions.rationale:
Option D is the key, and Ashvenor states it herself. Her test was to tape an accelerometer into a carrier and send it round the loop for a week; what the instrument gave back was that “the trace barely moved” between stations, with the one event worth naming falling at the end of the journey. She says as much: “It’s the stop at the far end that does it”. The remedy points the same way. The loop was left alone and the landing bins were changed, and it is after that change that “rejects are down by about half”. D restates the finding in different words, putting the damage in the arrival rather than in the distance covered.

Option A tempts because slowing a conveyance is the obvious cure for cargo that keeps breaking, and a fall in rejects is on the page, so anyone who has registered the fall without registering its cause will supply the likely-sounding reason. One sentence rules it out: “The loop runs at the speed it always has.” What changed was the bins, two of which are now lined with foam.

Option B tempts because the colour is the vivid thing here, and it is easy to carry it back up the chain to the ward, where the blood was taken. The colour is not available there: “Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning.” Whole blood is red throughout; the pink is visible only after the tube has been spun and the plasma has separated from the cells, which is the state of the tube Ashvenor holds to the window.

Option C takes a true thing about blood gases, that they cannot be left standing, and hangs the wrong conclusion on it, since urgent work is what a hospital would want a tube for. Their route is given the other way round: “Blood gases have never gone by tube; a porter walks those down.” The half that is true is what makes the whole of it tempting.

One direction in the mechanism is worth stating plainly, because it inverts easily. The cells break first, and their contents then pass into the plasma around them, which is why she says “their potassium is out in the plasma” and why the figure she would report comes out too high rather than too low. By the same route the pink is haemoglobin released from the cells, not something present in the tube beforehand.

generator_meta.topic: A hospital pneumatic-tube system and the samples it spoils. Red cells burst under the mechanical shock of transit; their potassium passes into the plasma, so the potassium figure reported runs high; free haemoglobin colours the spun plasma pink. A week with an accelerometer inside a carrier puts the shock at the receiving station rather than along the straight run, so foam-lined landing bins - not a slower loop - halve the rejects. Blood gases are kept out of the tube altogether.

generator_meta.mechanism_verification_note: Every causal direction in the passage and the rationale, stated so it can be checked (this is the axis batch21's short got wrong). (1) The red cells break FIRST, under mechanical shock; the potassium that was inside them then passes OUT into the plasma around them. Direction: cell -> plasma. Consequence: the potassium figure measured on that plasma is FALSELY HIGH, never falsely low, because intracellular potassium is far more concentrated than plasma potassium. The passage says 'their potassium is out in the plasma, so the number I'd report is higher than the patient's', and the rationale repeats the direction explicitly. (2) The PINK is free haemoglobin released from the same broken cells - not a property of the anticoagulant, not something added to the tube. The passage says 'That pink is haemoglobin, from the cells'. (3) The colour is invisible until the tube is SPUN, because whole blood is opaque red and the plasma has to be separated from the cells before its own colour can be seen; hence 'Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning' and the tube Ashvenor holds is a spun one. (4) The mechanical shock is greatest at the arrival, where the carrier's motion stops, not in the runs between stations where it travels at a steady speed; deceleration, not distance, is what the accelerometer records. This is why lining the landing bins - and not slowing the loop - is what halves the rejects, and the passage keeps the two apart. (5) The direction of the clinical consequence is also stated the right way round: a falsely high potassium produces a false ALARM about a patient who is fine, not a false reassurance about a patient who is not.
